title: Education Debates
subtitle: Argue about grades, selection and schooling itself — in balanced, well-hedged French

lessons.title: L'école en question
lessons.description: The three arguments that never stop in France: marks out of twenty, social mix in schools, and how long the school day should be.

blocks.heading: A country that argues about its school
blocks.body: In France, "l'École" with a capital E is not just a set of buildings — it is a republican institution, and touching it is political. Every government arrives with "une réforme" and leaves with "une contre-réforme" from the next one. The vocabulary of the debate is fixed: some speak of "l'égalité des chances", others of "le niveau qui baisse", and both camps claim to defend the same children. To argue at B2 you need the nouns, but above all the connectors that let you concede a point before answering it.

examples.french: Chaque ministre veut laisser son nom à une réforme.
examples.english: Every minister wants to leave their name on a reform.

examples.french: L'école républicaine promet l'égalité des chances.
examples.english: The republican school promises equality of opportunity.

examples.french: Les uns dénoncent la baisse du niveau, les autres la nostalgie.
examples.english: Some denounce falling standards, others nostalgia.
examples.note: "les uns… les autres…" balances two camps neatly

examples.french: Ce débat revient à chaque rentrée scolaire.
examples.english: This debate comes back every new school year.

examples.french: Il faudrait sortir des slogans et regarder les chiffres.
examples.english: We should get past the slogans and look at the figures.

examples.french: Sur ce point, les deux camps ont chacun une part de raison.
examples.english: On this point, each camp is partly right.
examples.note: "avoir une part de raison" — a very useful balanced formula

blocks.tip: Say "l'Éducation nationale" for the ministry and the system as a whole; "l'école" alone usually means primary school in everyday speech.

blocks.heading: Faut-il noter les élèves ?
blocks.body: French marks run "sur vingt", and almost nobody gets twenty. Critics of "la notation" argue that a mark ranks a child rather than describing what they can do, and that fear of the red pen kills curiosity. Defenders answer that a clear mark is honest, that removing it hides inequality instead of curing it, and that families and employers need a common measure. A middle position exists: "l'évaluation par compétences", where each skill is judged "acquis" or "en cours d'acquisition".

examples.french: Une note chiffrée classe l'élève plus qu'elle ne l'aide.
examples.english: A numerical mark ranks the pupil more than it helps them.
examples.note: "plus… que ne…" is the elegant comparative with expletive ne

examples.french: Supprimer les notes ne supprime pas les écarts.
examples.english: Removing marks does not remove the gaps.

examples.french: L'évaluation par compétences décrit ce que l'élève sait faire.
examples.english: Skills-based assessment describes what the pupil can do.

examples.french: Certains parents réclament un retour à la moyenne trimestrielle.
examples.english: Some parents are calling for a return to the termly average.

examples.french: Le contrôle continu réduit la pression d'un examen unique.
examples.english: Continuous assessment reduces the pressure of a single exam.

examples.french: On peut évaluer sans humilier, à condition d'être précis.
examples.english: You can assess without humiliating, provided you are precise.

blocks.tip: "Un zéro pointé" is the legendary flat zero. "Avoir la moyenne" means scraping 10/20 — the threshold every French pupil knows by heart.

blocks.heading: Mixité sociale et rythmes scolaires
blocks.body: Two other quarrels run in parallel. "La mixité sociale" asks whether children from different backgrounds actually sit in the same classroom; "la carte scolaire" assigns pupils to a school by address, which some call fair and others call a trap, since well-informed families find ways around it. Meanwhile "les rythmes scolaires" divide chronobiologists, mayors and exhausted parents: French pupils have few school days but very long ones, and every attempt to redistribute the week has ended in protest.

examples.french: La carte scolaire devait garantir la mixité sociale.
examples.english: The school catchment map was meant to guarantee social mixing.

examples.french: Les familles informées contournent la sectorisation.
examples.english: Well-informed families get around the catchment rules.

examples.french: Les journées françaises sont parmi les plus longues d'Europe.
examples.english: French school days are among the longest in Europe.

examples.french: La semaine de quatre jours arrange les parents, pas forcément les enfants.
examples.english: The four-day week suits parents, not necessarily children.

examples.french: Réformer les rythmes coûte cher aux communes.
examples.english: Reforming school hours is expensive for local councils.

examples.french: Quoi qu'on décide, une partie des parents sera mécontente.
examples.english: Whatever is decided, some parents will be unhappy.

blocks.tip: Don't confuse "la mixité" (boys and girls together, or social mixing) with "la mixité sociale" specifically — context decides, so add "sociale" when you mean backgrounds.

blocks.heading: Conceding before you object: bien que, quoique, même si
blocks.body: A balanced argument admits the other side first. "Bien que" and "quoique" both mean "although" and both take the subjunctive: "bien que la mesure soit coûteuse…". "Même si" means "even if / even though" and takes the indicative: "même si la mesure est coûteuse…". A third, very French option is "avoir beau" + infinitive: "on a beau critiquer les notes, elles rassurent les familles" — literally "however much people criticise marks". Choose "bien que" in writing, "même si" in speech.

examples.french: Bien que la réforme soit ambitieuse, elle manque de moyens.
examples.english: Although the reform is ambitious, it lacks resources.

examples.french: Quoique les résultats aient progressé, les écarts demeurent.
examples.english: Although results have improved, the gaps remain.

examples.french: Même si les notes stressent, elles restent lisibles pour tous.
examples.english: Even if marks are stressful, they remain readable for everyone.

examples.french: On a beau multiplier les circulaires, la pratique change lentement.
examples.english: However many circulars are issued, practice changes slowly.

examples.french: Elle a beau être expérimentée, elle prépare chaque cours.
examples.english: Experienced as she is, she prepares every lesson.

examples.french: Bien qu'il ait redoublé, il a obtenu son baccalauréat.
examples.english: Although he repeated a year, he passed his baccalauréat.

blocks.tip: Never say "bien que" + indicative in an exam. If the subjunctive form frightens you, rewrite with "même si" — it is correct, natural and safe.

blocks.heading: Nuancing an opinion: certes… mais, il n'en reste pas moins que
blocks.body: B2 debate is judged on nuance, not volume. "Certes… mais…" grants a point then turns: "Certes, les notes classent ; mais elles informent aussi." "Il n'en reste pas moins que" + indicative reasserts your point after a concession. To soften a claim, use "il semblerait que" + subjunctive, "on peut penser que" or "tout porte à croire que". To attribute an idea without endorsing it, use the conditional: "la réforme améliorerait les résultats" — reportedly, allegedly.

examples.french: Certes, la notation est brutale ; mais elle est transparente.
examples.english: Granted, grading is brutal; but it is transparent.

examples.french: Il n'en reste pas moins que les inégalités persistent.
examples.english: The fact remains that inequalities persist.

examples.french: Il semblerait que la mesure ait eu peu d'effet.
examples.english: It would appear that the measure had little effect.

examples.french: Selon le rapport, les résultats se seraient améliorés.
examples.english: According to the report, results have apparently improved.

examples.french: Tout porte à croire que le débat n'est pas clos.
examples.english: Everything suggests the debate is not over.

examples.french: On ne saurait réduire l'école à ses classements.
examples.english: One cannot reduce school to its rankings.

blocks.tip: In a written argument, one "certes… mais" per paragraph is plenty. Repeated, it makes you sound as if you never dare take a position.

items.tip: "Certes" is SEHRSS — the final -s is pronounced. Pause slightly after it, as French speakers do, before launching the concession.

passages.title: Conseil de classe, salle 12
passages.french:
Le conseil de classe commence à dix-sept heures trente, et la fatigue est déjà dans la pièce.
La professeure principale lit les moyennes à voix haute, colonne après colonne, sans commentaire.
« Onze virgule deux. Neuf virgule huit. Quatorze. » Personne ne réagit avant le troisième nom.
Un collègue finit par lever la main : « Ces chiffres, ils nous disent quoi, exactement ? »
La question n'est pas rhétorique, et elle revient chaque trimestre depuis trois ans.
D'un côté, ceux qui trouvent la note honnête : elle est claire, comparable, et les familles la comprennent tout de suite.
De l'autre, ceux qui la jugent injuste : elle classe un enfant au lieu de décrire ce qu'il sait faire.
« Un huit sur vingt n'a jamais appris à personne comment progresser », dit la professeure de lettres.
« Un « en cours d'acquisition » non plus, si on n'explique pas ce qui manque », répond son voisin de table.
La proviseure adjointe rappelle que l'établissement expérimente l'évaluation par compétences en sixième.
Les résultats sont, dit-elle, « encourageants mais fragiles » : les élèves stressent moins, les parents comprennent moins bien.
Une déléguée des élèves, seize ans, demande la parole et parle exactement quarante secondes.
« Ce qui nous angoisse, ce n'est pas la note. C'est de ne pas savoir ce qu'on attend de nous. »
Le silence qui suit dure plus longtemps que d'habitude, puis on passe au dossier suivant.
À dix-neuf heures, rien n'est tranché, et personne, en sortant, ne prétend le contraire.
passages.english:
The class council starts at half past five, and tiredness is already in the room.
The form teacher reads the averages out loud, column after column, without comment.
"Eleven point two. Nine point eight. Fourteen." Nobody reacts before the third name.
A colleague eventually raises his hand: "These figures — what exactly do they tell us?"
The question is not rhetorical, and it has come back every term for three years.
On one side, those who find the mark honest: it is clear, comparable, and families understand it immediately.
On the other, those who judge it unfair: it ranks a child instead of describing what they can do.
"An eight out of twenty has never taught anyone how to improve," says the literature teacher.
"Nor has an 'in progress', if you don't explain what is missing," replies the man beside her.
The deputy head reminds them that the school is trialling skills-based assessment in year seven.
The results, she says, are "encouraging but fragile": pupils are less stressed, parents understand less well.
A pupil representative, sixteen years old, asks to speak and talks for exactly forty seconds.
"What worries us is not the mark. It is not knowing what is expected of us."
The silence that follows lasts longer than usual, then they move on to the next file.
At seven o'clock, nothing has been settled, and nobody, on the way out, pretends otherwise.

lessons.title: L'université et la sélection
lessons.description: How French students get into higher education, why the word « sélection » is explosive, and how to argue about access without shouting.

blocks.heading: Two doors into higher education
blocks.body: French higher education has a split personality. "L'université" is open to anyone with the baccalauréat and charges only small "frais d'inscription"; "les grandes écoles" and "les classes préparatoires" recruit by "concours", a competitive exam with a fixed number of places. The result is a system that is officially open and practically hierarchical — which is exactly why the word "sélection" is so charged. Note the vocabulary trap: "un concours" ranks candidates against each other, whereas "un examen" only checks you against a standard.

examples.french: L'université est ouverte à tout bachelier.
examples.english: The university is open to anyone with the baccalauréat.

examples.french: Les grandes écoles recrutent sur concours.
examples.english: The grandes écoles recruit through competitive exams.

examples.french: On réussit un examen ; on est reçu à un concours.
examples.english: You pass an exam; you get through a competitive exam.

examples.french: Les classes préparatoires durent en général deux ans.
examples.english: Preparatory classes usually last two years.

examples.french: Les frais d'inscription restent modestes dans le public.
examples.english: Registration fees remain modest in the state sector.

examples.french: Le système est ouvert en droit, hiérarchisé en fait.
examples.english: The system is open in law, hierarchical in practice.
examples.note: "en droit… en fait…" is a classic argumentative pair

blocks.tip: "La fac" is the everyday word for university; "l'université" is the formal one. "Aller à la fac" ≠ "faire une prépa" — the two paths carry very different connotations.

blocks.heading: The algorithm everyone argues about
blocks.body: Since 2018 a national platform assigns places: pupils enter "des vœux", each course examines "les dossiers", and answers come back as "oui", "oui si" (accepted with support) or "en attente" (waitlisted). Defenders say it replaced a lottery with an honest look at each file and finally tells students what a course demands. Critics answer that judging seventeen-year-olds on their school reports rewards those from well-informed families, and that weeks of waiting are cruel. Both sides agree on one thing: the previous system was worse.

examples.french: Elle a formulé dix vœux sur la plateforme.
examples.english: She entered ten choices on the platform.

examples.french: Son dossier a été classé en liste d'attente.
examples.english: Her application was placed on the waiting list.

examples.french: Un « oui si » impose un parcours d'accompagnement.
examples.english: A conditional yes imposes a support programme.

examples.french: Les attendus de la formation sont publiés à l'avance.
examples.english: The course requirements are published in advance.

examples.french: Le tirage au sort avait été jugé absurde par tout le monde.
examples.english: The lottery had been judged absurd by everyone.

examples.french: L'algorithme n'invente pas les inégalités, il les révèle.
examples.english: The algorithm does not invent inequalities, it reveals them.
examples.note: a common nuanced position in the debate

blocks.tip: Say "formuler un vœu" (to enter a choice), not "faire un vœu" — the latter means making a wish on a birthday candle.

blocks.heading: Arguing about access without slogans
blocks.body: Two principles collide. "L'égalité d'accès" says that a public university funded by everyone should turn nobody away; "la réussite" says that admitting students to a course they will fail is a cruel form of generosity, since first-year failure rates are high. Between the two sits "l'orientation": better information earlier, so that choices are informed rather than filtered. When you argue at B2, name the value behind each position — that is what raises your register above "c'est injuste".

examples.french: Le taux d'échec en première année reste préoccupant.
examples.english: The first-year failure rate remains worrying.

examples.french: Ouvrir l'accès sans accompagner, est-ce vraiment égalitaire ?
examples.english: Is opening access without support really egalitarian?

examples.french: Chacun défend une valeur : l'égalité pour les uns, la réussite pour les autres.
examples.english: Each side defends a value: equality for some, success for others.

examples.french: Une bonne orientation vaut mieux qu'une sélection tardive.
examples.english: Good guidance is worth more than late selection.

examples.french: Les boursiers bénéficient de quotas dans certaines filières.
examples.english: Scholarship students benefit from quotas in some courses.

examples.french: Il ne s'agit pas de trancher, mais de peser les arguments.
examples.english: It is not about settling the matter, but weighing the arguments.

blocks.tip: "La sélection" is a fighting word in French politics. Neutral alternatives exist: "le recrutement", "l'admission", "les capacités d'accueil" — choose deliberately.

blocks.heading: Hypothesis and consequence: si, au cas où, à condition que
blocks.body: Arguing about policy means arguing about what would happen. "Si" + imparfait → conditionnel présent describes an unreal present: "si l'accès était totalement libre, les amphithéâtres déborderaient". "Si" + plus-que-parfait → conditionnel passé judges the past: "si on l'avait mieux orienté, il n'aurait pas abandonné". Two useful cousins: "au cas où" takes the conditional ("au cas où tu serais refusé"), and "à condition que" takes the subjunctive ("à condition que l'université soit financée").

examples.french: Si l'accès était totalement libre, les capacités seraient dépassées.
examples.english: If access were completely open, capacity would be exceeded.

blocks.tip: Never write "si j'aurais" — the conditional never follows "si". The only exception is indirect question: "je me demande si j'aurais réussi".

blocks.heading: Impersonal structures for formal argument
blocks.body: Formal French prefers "il" to "je". "Il convient de", "il importe de", "il s'agit de" and "force est de constater que" let you assert without exposing yourself. Watch the mood: "il est vrai que" and "il est certain que" take the indicative, but their negatives and "il est possible / souhaitable / regrettable que" take the subjunctive. And "il s'agit de" is impersonal only — never "cette réforme s'agit de".

passages.title: Le mois de mai de Camille
passages.french:
Camille a dix-sept ans, dix vœux formulés, et un téléphone qu'elle regarde toutes les onze minutes.
Elle vise une licence de psychologie ; sa formation reçoit onze candidatures pour une place.
« Je ne demande pas d'être prise, dit-elle. Je demande de savoir. Attendre, c'est ça le plus dur. »
Son professeur principal, lui, défend le système sans enthousiasme excessif.
« Avant, on tirait au sort. Un ordinateur décidait de l'avenir d'un élève à pile ou face. Personne ne veut revenir à ça. »
La conseillère d'orientation nuance : les attendus sont publiés, certes, mais encore faut-il savoir les lire.
« Les familles qui connaissent le système placent leurs vœux avec méthode. Les autres découvrent les règles en juin. »
À l'université, le doyen rappelle un chiffre que l'on cite rarement dans les débats télévisés.
Moins d'un étudiant sur deux obtient sa licence en trois ans, et l'abandon se joue souvent dès le premier semestre.
« Accueillir tout le monde sans moyens supplémentaires, ce n'est pas de l'égalité, c'est de l'affichage », dit-il.
Une étudiante de deuxième année, boursière, n'est pas d'accord : elle serait passée à côté de tout si l'entrée avait été sélective.
« On m'aurait regardé mon dossier de terminale et on m'aurait dit non. Aujourd'hui je suis dans les meilleures. »
Le débat s'arrête là où il commence toujours : sur ce que l'on accepte de financer.
Camille, elle, a reçu une réponse le douze juin, à vingt-deux heures quatre.
C'était « oui si », avec un tutorat obligatoire le mercredi. Elle a accepté sans réfléchir longtemps.
passages.english:
Camille is seventeen, has entered ten choices, and looks at her phone every eleven minutes.
She is aiming for a psychology degree; her course receives eleven applications per place.
"I'm not asking to get in," she says. "I'm asking to know. The waiting is the hardest part."
Her form teacher, for his part, defends the system without excessive enthusiasm.
"Before, they drew lots. A computer decided a pupil's future on a coin toss. Nobody wants to go back to that."
The careers adviser adds a qualification: the course requirements are published, granted, but you still have to know how to read them.
"Families who know the system place their choices methodically. The others discover the rules in June."
At the university, the dean recalls a figure rarely quoted in televised debates.
Fewer than one student in two gets their degree in three years, and dropping out is often decided in the first semester.
"Taking everyone in without extra resources is not equality, it is window dressing," he says.
A second-year student on a grant disagrees: she would have missed out on everything if entry had been selective.
"They'd have looked at my final-year school report and said no. Today I'm among the best."
The debate stops where it always starts: on what we agree to pay for.
Camille got an answer on the twelfth of June, at four minutes past ten in the evening.
It was a conditional yes, with compulsory tutoring on Wednesdays. She accepted without thinking about it for long.

lessons.title: Éduquer autrement
lessons.description: Montessori, Freinet, home schooling: the vocabulary of alternative pedagogies and the arguments made for and against them.

blocks.heading: The alternative family tree
blocks.body: "Les pédagogies alternatives" are older than they look. Maria Montessori built "l'autonomie" into the furniture itself; Célestin Freinet put a printing press in a village classroom and had children publish their own texts; Rudolf Steiner tied learning to artistic rhythm. What they share is a shift of centre: the child's activity rather than the teacher's lesson. What they do not share is a single doctrine — so avoid saying "la pédagogie alternative" in the singular, as if one method existed.

examples.french: Les pédagogies alternatives placent l'enfant au centre.
examples.english: Alternative pedagogies place the child at the centre.

examples.french: Le matériel Montessori est conçu pour être manipulé seul.
examples.english: Montessori materials are designed to be handled alone.

examples.french: Freinet faisait imprimer aux élèves leur propre journal.
examples.english: Freinet had pupils print their own newspaper.

examples.french: L'apprentissage se fait par l'expérience plutôt que par la leçon.
examples.english: Learning happens through experience rather than through the lesson.

examples.french: Ces courants n'ont ni la même origine ni les mêmes objectifs.
examples.english: These currents have neither the same origin nor the same aims.

examples.french: Beaucoup d'écoles publiques empruntent certaines de ces pratiques.
examples.english: Many state schools borrow some of these practices.

blocks.tip: "Une école Montessori" is not a protected label in France — the name is not trademarked as a school certification, so quality varies enormously from one school to the next.

blocks.heading: L'instruction en famille
blocks.body: In French law, schooling is not compulsory — "l'instruction" is. That distinction is what allows "l'instruction en famille", teaching your children at home. Since 2021 it requires prior authorisation rather than a simple declaration, on grounds such as health, a sporting career, or a documented educational project. Supporters see a fundamental parental freedom and a remedy for children whom school makes miserable; opponents worry about isolation, uneven monitoring and the loss of a shared civic space.

examples.french: En France, l'instruction est obligatoire, pas l'école.
examples.english: In France, education is compulsory, not school.

examples.french: L'instruction en famille est désormais soumise à autorisation.
examples.english: Home education is now subject to authorisation.

examples.french: Un inspecteur vérifie chaque année les progrès de l'enfant.
examples.english: An inspector checks the child's progress every year.

examples.french: Certains parents invoquent le harcèlement subi à l'école.
examples.english: Some parents cite bullying suffered at school.

examples.french: D'autres craignent l'isolement social des enfants concernés.
examples.english: Others fear the social isolation of the children involved.

examples.french: Le débat oppose liberté familiale et protection de l'enfant.
examples.english: The debate pits family freedom against child protection.

blocks.tip: Say "l'instruction en famille" (abbreviated IEF) rather than the calque "l'école à la maison" if you want to sound informed — though the second is what people say in conversation.

blocks.heading: Weighing the arguments fairly
blocks.body: The honest version of this debate has evidence problems on both sides. Advocates point to "l'épanouissement", "la motivation intrinsèque" and children who read because they want to. Sceptics note that comparative studies are hard to run, that families choosing these schools are rarely representative, and that a warm classroom is not automatically an effective one. A useful B2 move is to separate the claim about values ("what should school be for?") from the claim about results ("does it work?") — they are argued differently.

examples.french: Les partisans invoquent l'épanouissement et la motivation.
examples.english: Supporters invoke fulfilment and motivation.

examples.french: Les détracteurs réclament des études comparatives sérieuses.
examples.english: Critics call for serious comparative studies.

blocks.heading: Purpose and consequence: pour que, afin que, si bien que
blocks.body: Alternative pedagogies are always described by their aims, so you need purpose clauses. "Pour que" and "afin que" express purpose and take the subjunctive: "afin que l'enfant apprenne seul". When the subject is the same on both sides, drop the clause entirely and use "pour" / "afin de" + infinitive: "il range son matériel pour retrouver ses repères". Consequence works the other way round and takes the indicative: "si bien que", "de sorte que", "au point que". Beware "de sorte que", which switches to the subjunctive when it means purpose rather than result.

blocks.tip: "Pour que" is never followed by the indicative. If you catch yourself writing "pour que l'enfant apprend", stop and check whether the subject really changes — if not, "pour apprendre" is simpler and correct.

blocks.heading: Reporting and distancing what others claim
blocks.body: In a balanced discussion you constantly report claims you neither endorse nor reject. Use "selon", "d'après", "aux dires de" to attribute; use the conditional to mark uncertainty ("la méthode favoriserait l'autonomie"); use "prétendre" for a claim you doubt and "soutenir" or "affirmer" for a neutral one. Remember that "prétendre" means "to claim (dubiously)", not "to pretend" — a false friend that changes the temperature of a whole sentence.

examples.french: Selon ses partisans, la méthode favoriserait l'autonomie.
examples.english: According to its supporters, the method reportedly fosters independence.

examples.french: D'après le rapport, les résultats seraient comparables.
examples.english: According to the report, results are apparently comparable.

examples.french: Ils prétendent que l'école tue la créativité.
examples.english: They claim that school kills creativity.

examples.french: Les chercheurs soutiennent que les données manquent.
examples.english: Researchers maintain that the data are lacking.

examples.french: Il affirme avoir constaté une nette amélioration.
examples.english: He states that he observed a clear improvement.

examples.french: Rien ne permet d'affirmer que la méthode soit supérieure.
examples.english: Nothing allows us to claim that the method is superior.

blocks.tip: The conditional of report — "favoriserait", "seraient" — is the single most useful tool for staying neutral. Journalists use it constantly; so should you in an argumentative essay.

items.prompt: Express a purpose with 'pour que'.

items.english: The furniture is adapted so that the child becomes independent.
items.tip: "Devienne" is duh-VYEN — one clean nasal-free ending, unlike "deviennent" which sounds identical. Keep "pour que" short and unstressed.

items.prompt: Report a claim without endorsing it.
items.french: D'après ses partisans, cette méthode favoriserait la créativité.
items.english: According to its supporters, this method reportedly fosters creativity.
items.tip: Stress the ending of "favoriserait" — fah-voh-ree-zuh-REH — so the conditional is audible. That ending is what signals your distance.

items.prompt: State the counter-argument neutrally.

items.english: Social isolation remains the main risk raised by critics.
items.tip: "Isolement" has four syllables: ee-zol-MAHN, with no sound between the l and the -ement. Don't add an English "aisle".

passages.title: Deux tables, deux convictions
passages.french:
Dans la classe de Nour, il n'y a pas de rangées : douze enfants, quatre îlots, et beaucoup de matériel en bois.
À neuf heures, chacun choisit son activité et personne ne lève la main pour demander la permission.
« Ce que je veux, dit l'enseignante, c'est qu'ils apprennent à décider. Le reste vient ensuite. »
À trois rues de là, dans une école publique de quartier, Sofiane défend une conviction différente.
« On m'a beaucoup expliqué que la contrainte tue la curiosité. Je vois surtout des enfants rassurés par un cadre. »
Il ne critique pas les pédagogies alternatives ; il conteste l'idée qu'elles conviendraient à tous.
« Douze élèves et deux adultes, évidemment que cela marche. Donnez-moi les mêmes moyens et nous en reparlerons. »
L'argument revient souvent, et les partisans de ces méthodes ne le balaient pas.
Certains reconnaissent volontiers que les familles concernées sont rarement représentatives de la population.
D'autres répondent que des écoles publiques appliquent ces principes depuis des décennies, sans effectifs réduits.
Le débat sur l'instruction en famille est plus tendu encore, parce qu'il touche à la liberté des parents.
Une mère explique qu'elle a déscolarisé son fils après deux ans de harcèlement, et qu'on ne lui fera pas la leçon.
Une inspectrice rappelle, sans hausser le ton, que le contrôle annuel existe pour l'enfant, pas contre la famille.
Aucun des deux n'a tort, et c'est précisément ce qui rend la discussion difficile.
À midi, Nour range son matériel et Sofiane corrige des dictées, chacun convaincu de faire au mieux.
passages.english:
In Nour's class there are no rows: twelve children, four clusters of tables, and a lot of wooden equipment.
At nine o'clock, everyone chooses their activity and nobody raises a hand to ask permission.
"What I want," says the teacher, "is for them to learn to decide. The rest comes afterwards."
Three streets away, in a neighbourhood state school, Sofiane defends a different conviction.
"I've been told a lot that constraint kills curiosity. What I mostly see is children reassured by a framework."
He does not criticise alternative pedagogies; he disputes the idea that they would suit everyone.
"Twelve pupils and two adults — of course it works. Give me the same resources and we'll talk again."
The argument comes up often, and supporters of these methods do not brush it aside.
Some readily acknowledge that the families involved are rarely representative of the population.
Others reply that state schools have been applying these principles for decades, without small class sizes.
The debate on home education is tenser still, because it touches on parents' freedom.
One mother explains that she took her son out of school after two years of bullying, and that nobody will lecture her.
An inspector points out, without raising her voice, that the annual check exists for the child, not against the family.
Neither of them is wrong, and that is precisely what makes the discussion difficult.
At midday Nour tidies her equipment and Sofiane marks dictations, each convinced they are doing their best.
